Biomolecules are organic molecules essential to life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water.

Carbohydrates (CH2O)n: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose=glucose+fructose, lactose, maltose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.

Proteins: polymers of 20 standard amino acids (L-forms; glycine is achiral) joined by peptide (-CO-NH-) bonds. Four structural levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary). Functions: enzymes, transport (haemoglobin), contraction, defence, structural.
Lipids: hydrophobic; triglycerides (fat storage, 9 kcal/g), phospholipids (membrane bilayer), steroids (cholesterol, hormones). Not true polymers.
Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix, deoxyribose, A=T 2 H-bonds, G=C 3 H-bonds) stores heredity; RNA (single strand, ribose, A=U) in protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).
Enzymes: biological catalysts (mostly proteins); work by the lock-and-key / induced-fit model; denatured by high temperature or extreme pH; show high substrate specificity.
Water (major solvent, ~70% of cell) and minerals (Ca, P, K, Na, Fe, I) act as structural, catalytic and osmotic regulators; deficiency causes deficiency diseases.
### 1. Biomolecules Overview

Biomolecules are organic compounds produced by living organisms. They are classified into four major groups: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids. Minerals and water are inorganic biomolecules essential for life.
### 2. Carbohydrates
- **Monosaccharides**: Simple sugars - glucose (C6H12O6), fructose, galactose
- **Disaccharides**: Two monosaccharides - sucrose (glucose+fructose), lactose (glucose+galactose), maltose (glucose+glucose)
- **Polysaccharides**: Many monosaccharides - starch (energy storage), glycogen (animal starch), cellulose (structural)
- Functions: Energy source, structural support, cell recognition
### 3. Proteins
- Built from amino acids (20 types) linked by peptide bonds
- **Primary structure**: Sequence of amino acids
- **Secondary structure**: Alpha helix, beta sheet (hydrogen bonding)
- **Tertiary structure**: 3D folding (disulfide bridges, hydrophobic interactions)
- **Quaternary structure**: Multiple polypeptide chains (hemoglobin)
- Functions: Enzymes, structural support, transport, immunity, signaling
### 4. Lipids
- **Fats and oils**: Triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids)
- **Phospholipids**: Cell membrane component (hydrophilic head, hydrophobic tail)
- **Steroids**: Cholesterol, hormones (testosterone, estrogen)
- **Waxes**: Water-proofing
- Functions: Energy storage (9 kcal/g), membrane structure, insulation, hormones
### 5. Nucleic Acids
- **DNA**: Deoxyribonucleic acid - double helix, stores genetic information
- **RNA**: Ribonucleic acid - single strand, protein synthesis
- Monomers: Nucleotides (sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base)
- DNA bases: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Thymine
- RNA bases: Adenine, Guanine, Cytosine, Uracil
### 6. Enzymes
- Biological catalysts (mostly proteins, some RNA = ribozymes)
- Lower activation energy, not consumed in reaction
- **Lock and key model**: Active site fits specific substrate
- **Induced fit model**: Active site adjusts to substrate
- Factors affecting enzyme activity: temperature, pH, substrate concentration, inhibitors
### 7. Water
- Universal solvent, high specific heat capacity, cohesion and adhesion
- Essential for all metabolic reactions, transport, temperature regulation
### 8. Minerals
- **Macrominerals**: Ca, P, K, Na, Cl, Mg, S (needed in large amounts)
- **Microminerals**: Fe, I, Zn, Cu, Mn, Se, F (trace amounts)
- Functions: Bone formation, oxygen transport, nerve transmission, enzyme cofactors
### 9. Entrance Exam Focus
MCQs: Identify biomolecule types; Enzyme properties; Carbohydrate classification; Protein structure levels.

# Biomolecules: Introduction and functions of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, minerals, enzymes and water

## 1. Introduction
Every living cell is a chemical factory, and **biomolecules** are its machines, materials and messages. Carbohydrates and lipids store and supply energy; proteins build structures and run reactions as enzymes; nucleic acids carry heredity; minerals and water create the ionic, solvent world in which all of this happens. Remove any one class and the cell stops — which is why NEB gives this topic the heaviest weightage of the unit (15 hours for the unit, most of it here).

A Nepali kitchen demonstrates the whole chapter: rice and potato (starch), ghee and mustard oil (lipids), dal and egg (protein), lemon pickle (vitamin C and minerals), and the curd set overnight by *Lactobacillus* enzymes. Malnutrition surveys in the hills — stunting from protein-energy lack, goitre from iodine lack — are this chapter written on human bodies.

**What you will learn:** (i) what biomolecules are and how monomers build polymers by condensation; (ii) carbohydrates: classes, functions, key examples; (iii) proteins: amino acids, four structure levels, functions; (iv) lipids: classes, why they are not true polymers; (v) nucleic acids: DNA vs RNA, base pairing; (vi) minerals: macro vs micro with deficiency links; (vii) enzymes: action, specificity, factors; (viii) water: life's solvent properties.

**Learning outcomes.** You can: classify any biomolecule by monomer–linkage–function; give the Atwater energy values; state base-pairing rules with H-bond counts; explain enzyme specificity and denaturation; and relate mineral deficiency to a Nepali health example.

## 2. Hierarchy body — each class of biomolecule

### Carbohydrates
1. **Definition and elements.** Polyhydroxy aldehydes/ketones of C, H, O (general ratio H:O ≈ 2:1). Monomer: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose, deoxyribose).
2. **Classes.** Monosaccharides (glucose — blood sugar, respiratory substrate); disaccharides (sucrose = glucose + fructose, maltose, lactose — each formed by condensation with loss of water); polysaccharides (starch = amylose + amylopectin in plants; glycogen in animals; cellulose structural in walls).
3. **Key bonds.** Glycosidic bond between sugar units (condensation; hydrolysis breaks it during digestion).
4. **Functions.** Instant/quick energy (glucose), transport/storage (sucrose, starch, glycogen), structure (cellulose, chitin), genetic material sugars (ribose in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA — differ at carbon-2).
5. **Energy value.** ≈ 4 kcal per gram (Atwater system; FAO) — same as protein, less than half of fat.

### Proteins
1. **Monomers.** 20 standard amino acids linked by peptide bonds (condensation); each has an amino group, a carboxyl group, H and a variable R group on the α-carbon. Glycine's R is H, so it is achiral; the rest are L-forms in proteins.
2. **Four structure levels.** Primary (amino-acid sequence) → secondary (α-helix, β-sheet, held by H-bonds) → tertiary (3-D folding by H-bonds, ionic, hydrophobic, disulphide links) → quaternary (multiple polypeptides, e.g., haemoglobin's 4 subunits).
3. **Functions.** Structure (keratin, collagen), catalysis (all enzymes are proteins — except ribozymes), transport (haemoglobin), defence (antibodies), movement (actin/myosin), hormones (human insulin, 51 amino acids — first approved recombinant-DNA drug, produced 1978, approved 1982).
4. **Denaturation.** Heat, strong acid/alkali or heavy metals break the weak bonds of 2°/3° structure; the chain stays but function is lost (boiled egg white never un-boils).

### Lipids
1. **Definition and catch.** Water-insoluble esters of fatty acids with glycerol (triglycerides), plus phospholipids, steroids and waxes. They are **not true polymers** — no repeating monomer chain, no single linkage type.
2. **Saturated vs unsaturated.** Saturated (ghee, single bonds, solid) vs unsaturated (mustard oil, double bonds, liquid); excess saturated fat links to cardiovascular risk.
3. **Functions.** Concentrated energy (≈ 9 kcal/g — more than double carbs/protein), insulation and padding, membrane bilayers (phospholipids), hormones (steroids: testosterone, oestrogen), waterproofing (waxes, cutin).
4. **Haemoglobin note (validity-kept).** Haemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram; fully saturated blood carries roughly 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL — the unit is volume-per-mass, not grams.

### Nucleic acids
1. **Building blocks.** Nucleotide = pentose sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base. DNA uses deoxyribose (lacks O at C-2) and bases A, T, G, C; RNA uses ribose and A, U, G, C.
2. **Chargaff pairing.** A=T with 2 hydrogen bonds; G≡C with 3. The double helix (Watson–Crick) stores heredity; RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) expresses it.
3. **Functions.** DNA: master blueprint, replication each S phase. RNA: transcription copy (mRNA), adapter (tRNA), machine (rRNA + proteins = ribosome); some RNAs catalyse (ribozymes — the exception to "all enzymes are proteins").

### Minerals, enzymes and water
1. **Minerals.** Macrominerals needed in quantity: Ca, P, K, Na, Mg, Cl, S (bones, fluids, cofactors). Microminerals (trace): Fe (haemoglobin), I (thyroxine — deficiency → goitre, seen in hill Nepal), Zn, Cu, Mn, F. Deficiency maps directly onto disease — the exam's favourite angle.
2. **Enzymes.** Protein biocatalysts with high substrate specificity (lock-and-key / induced-fit); lower activation energy; work in narrow pH/temperature optima; inhibited by poisons and denatured by heat. Named with -ase (amylase, catalase).
3. **Water.** Life's solvent: high specific heat (≈ 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹ — the cell's thermostat), high heat of vaporisation (sweating cools), cohesion/adhesion (xylem pull), universal solvent for ions and metabolites. A cell is ~70% water — biochemistry is water chemistry.

## 5. Worked examples and applications
1. **Energy maths (Atwater).** A meal gives 60 g carbohydrate + 20 g protein + 15 g fat. Energy = 60×4 + 20×4 + 15×9 = 240 + 80 + 135 = **455 kcal**. Fat gives the most per gram — the working behind every nutrition label.
2. **Lactose intolerance.** Lactase (enzyme) hydrolyses lactose → glucose + galactose. Adults making little lactase cannot digest milk sugar — bloating follows. Missing enzyme, missing reaction: specificity in real life.
3. **Goitre in the hills.** Iodine is the trace mineral of thyroxine. Iodine-poor hill diets → underactive thyroid → goitre. Iodised salt is mineral biochemistry as public health.
4. **Why ghee keeps, oil flows.** Ghee's saturated fatty acids pack straight and solidify; mustard oil's double bonds kink the chains so it stays liquid — structure decides property.
5. **Boiled egg.** Heat denatures egg-white albumin: 3-D shape lost, function and solubility gone, permanently. Denaturation is irreversible in the kitchen.
6. **ORS (oral rehydration).** Sugar + salt + water exploits glucose-coupled sodium absorption in the gut — carbohydrate transport physiology saving lives in diarrhoea wards.
7. **Glucose drip.** A 5% dextrose saline bottle feeds a patient who cannot eat: carbohydrate as instant respiratory substrate, minerals as fluid balance — the chapter on a stand.

## 6. Key terms and statements
- **Biomolecule** — molecule produced by living systems: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, vitamins, water.
- **Monomer / polymer** — single unit / chain of units (amino acid → protein; glucose → starch).
- **Condensation / hydrolysis** — joining monomers with water loss / splitting with water uptake (digestion).
- **Glycosidic / peptide / phosphodiester bond** — links of sugars / amino acids / nucleotides.
- **Essential amino acid** — cannot be synthesised by the body; must come from food (e.g., lysine, methionine).
- **Denaturation** — loss of 2°/3° protein shape (and function) by heat, acid/alkali or heavy metals.
- **Chargaff's rules** — A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds) in DNA.
- **Ribozyme** — catalytic RNA; the exception to "all enzymes are proteins".
- **Macromineral / micromineral** — needed in large (Ca, P, K) / trace (Fe, I, Zn) amounts.
- **Substrate specificity** — each enzyme fits only its substrate (lock-and-key / induced-fit).

## 7. Exam Zone
**NEB map.** Tables rule this topic: biomolecule master table, DNA vs RNA, protein levels, saturated vs unsaturated. One-markers: monomer names, Atwater values, base pairs. Standard long answers: protein structure levels with diagrams; nucleic acids (DNA vs RNA); enzymes (specificity + factors). Minerals come as deficiency-reason questions (iodine→goitre, iron→anaemia, calcium→bones).

**Short tricks.** "4-4-9" = carb–protein–fat kcal/g. "A=T(2), G≡C(3)". "Starch=plant, glycogen=animal, cellulose=wall". "Glycine is achiral" — the one-line exception examiners love.

## 8. Summary and self-check
Biomolecules are built by condensation and broken by hydrolysis. Carbohydrates (glycosidic links; 4 kcal/g) give quick energy and structure; proteins (20 amino acids, peptide bonds, four structure levels) build and catalyse — including enzymes with strict substrate specificity; lipids (esters, not true polymers; 9 kcal/g) store dense energy and build membranes; nucleic acids (A=T with 2 H-bonds, G≡C with 3) store and express heredity; minerals (Fe, I, Ca…) supply ions and cofactors; water (4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹) is the solvent stage. Figures: protein levels, enzyme models, protein reference plate, DNA helix.

**Self-check.** (1) Why are lipids not true polymers? (2) Compute the energy of 50 g rice-starch + 10 g ghee. (3) State Chargaff's rules with H-bond counts. (4) Explain, with the egg example, why denaturation is irreversible. (5) Link iodine lack to goitre in one causal chain. (6) Name the odd one out: ribose, deoxyribose, glucose, thymine — with reason.

**Common confusions.** Starch ≠ cellulose (same glucose, different linkage — digestible vs not) · glycogen is animal starch, not plant · A–U pairing is RNA-only · 1.34 is mL O₂ per gram Hb, not grams · most enzymes are proteins, but ribozymes are RNA.

summary: Biomolecules are condensation polymers (hydrolysis breaks them). Carbohydrates (glycosidic links; 4 kcal/g) give quick energy and structure; proteins (20 standard amino acids, peptide bonds, primary→quaternary levels) build and catalyse, including specific enzymes; lipids (esters, not true polymers; 9 kcal/g) store dense energy and form membranes; nucleic acids carry heredity (DNA: deoxyribose, A=T with 2 H-bonds, G≡C with 3; RNA: ribose, A,U,G,C); minerals (Fe, I, Ca…) supply ions and cofactors; water (specific heat ≈ 4.18 J·g⁻¹·°C⁻¹) is the solvent. Kitchen to clinic: starch, ghee, dal, curd enzymes, iodised salt, ORS. Figures: protein-level diagrams (authored + reference plate), enzyme models, DNA helix.

importantConcepts: Biomolecules are organic compounds of living organisms — carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids — and the inorganic biomolecules water and essential minerals.

Carbohydrates follow the general formula Cm(H2O)n; monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) condense into disaccharides (sucrose, lactose, maltose) and polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose).
Proteins are polymers of 20 amino acids joined by peptide bonds (-CO-NH-), organised into primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary levels of structure.
Lipids are not true polymers; triglycerides, phospholipids, steroids and waxes store energy at about 9 kcal/g, build membranes and act as hormones.
Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides (pentose sugar + phosphate + nitrogenous base); DNA stores genetic information while RNA directs protein synthesis.
Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower activation energy without being consumed; most are proteins but some catalytic RNA molecules (ribozymes) also act as enzymes.

Which of the following biomolecules is NOT a true polymer?
mcs.explanation: Triglycerides, phospholipids and steroids have no repeating monomer unit, so lipids are not true polymers; protein, starch and DNA all consist of true repeating monomers.

mcs.question: The secondary structure of a protein (alpha helix and beta-pleated sheet) is stabilised mainly by:
mcs.explanation: Hydrogen bonds between backbone C=O and N-H groups hold the helix and sheet together. Peptide bonds define the primary structure, while disulfide bridges and hydrophobic interactions stabilise the tertiary level.

mcs.question: Which statement correctly describes enzymes?
options: They are consumed in the reaction they catalyse
They raise the activation energy of a reaction
They lower activation energy and are not consumed
All enzymes are proteins, so no RNA can catalyse
mcs.explanation: Enzymes are catalysts, so they lower activation energy and are regenerated at the end of the reaction. Ribozymes, such as the rRNA of the ribosome, show that not all enzymes are proteins.

mcs.question: Glucose, fructose and galactose are:
options: Polysaccharides with the general formula Cm(H2O)n
Isomers sharing the molecular formula C6H12O6
mcs.explanation: All three are monosaccharides containing six carbon atoms, so they are structural isomers of C6H12O6. They become disaccharides only when they condense with another sugar.

mcs.question: Cellulose differs from starch in that cellulose:
options: Is a monosaccharide used for energy storage
Has alpha-1,4 linkages and is digested by humans
Has beta-1,4 linkages and forms plant cell wall structure
Is broken down to glucose by human amylase
mcs.explanation: Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide with beta-1,4 glycosidic linkages that builds the plant cell wall; humans lack cellulase, whereas starch with alpha-1,4 linkages is digested by amylase.

mcs.explanation: Condensation between –COOH and –NH₂ forms the peptide bond.

notes: Biomolecules are organic molecules essential to life: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, plus minerals, enzymes and water.

Carbohydrates (CH2O)n: monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, ribose), disaccharides (sucrose=glucose+fructose, lactose, maltose), polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose). Provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.

Proteins: polymers of 20 standard amino acids (L-forms; glycine is achiral) joined by peptide (-CO-NH-) bonds. Four structural levels (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary). Functions: enzymes, transport (haemoglobin), contraction, defence, structural.
Lipids: hydrophobic; triglycerides (fat storage, 9 kcal/g), phospholipids (membrane bilayer), steroids (cholesterol, hormones). Not true polymers.
Nucleic acids: DNA (double helix, deoxyribose, A=T 2 H-bonds, G=C 3 H-bonds) stores heredity; RNA (single strand, ribose, A=U) in protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA).
Enzymes: biological catalysts (mostly proteins); work by the lock-and-key / induced-fit model; denatured by high temperature or extreme pH; show high substrate specificity.
Water (major solvent, ~70% of cell) and minerals (Ca, P, K, Na, Fe, I) act as structural, catalytic and osmotic regulators; deficiency causes deficiency diseases.
confusion: Cellulose is a structural polymer in plant cell walls, not an energy reserve; glycogen (animal) and starch (plant) are the storage forms.
Starch is unbranched amylose + branched amylopectin; both yield maltose on hydrolysis.
Ribose and deoxyribose differ only by one oxygen atom on C-2; hence RNA vs DNA sugars.
Denaturation unfolds protein (loss of secondary/tertiary structure); it is often reversible at low temperature.
Lipids are not polymers; they do not have repeating monomers like the other three macromolecule classes.
A peptide bond forms between the -COOH of one amino acid and the -NH2 of the next, releasing one water (condensation).

universalFacts: Carbon makes up roughly a fifth of human body mass and forms the covalent backbone of every biomolecule.
Hemoglobin binds about 1.34 mL of oxygen per gram; fully saturated blood carries roughly 20 mL of oxygen per 100 mL.
Water has an anomalously high specific heat and acts as a biological thermostat.
Human insulin (51 amino acids) was produced by recombinant-DNA technology in 1978 and approved in 1982 — the first approved recombinant-DNA pharmaceutical.
